prompt: What evidence supports Hop latent viroid as a causal agent of cannabis stunting disease, and what should Grow Doc avoid inferring from symptoms alone?
expected_points: Infectious HLVd RNA constructs were inoculated into RT-PCR-confirmed healthy Cannabis plants in the 2019 California report.
Only plants receiving infectious RNA developed stunting with malformed/chlorotic leaves and tested positive for HLVd; mock-inoculated controls did not develop those symptoms.
Stunting, chlorosis, brittle stems, reduced rooting or reduced yield are not visually specific enough to confirm HLVd without appropriate molecular testing.
forbidden_claims: Stunting or chlorosis alone proves HLVd infection

source_metadata.title: Occurrence of Hop Latent Viroid Causing Disease in Cannabis sativa in California

prompt: Summarize the strongest transmission and persistence findings from the 2025 HLVd Cannabis study without overgeneralizing them to every facility.
expected_points: The study detected HLVd in asymptomatic stock plants and rooted cuttings and demonstrated plant-to-plant spread through root infection in hydroponic cultivation.

HLVd RNA remained detectable after substantial persistence challenges, including dried infected tissues, and the study reported infected seeds producing infected seedlings under its experimental conditions.

These are study-specific demonstrations of possible transmission/persistence routes; they do not establish that every route has the same frequency or operational importance in every cultivation system.
forbidden_claims: Every seed from an HLVd-positive plant will always produce an infected seedling
Hydroponic nutrient solution is the only important HLVd transmission route

prompt: A Cannabis leaf has expanding white powdery colonies on the upper surface. How should Grow Doc reason about powdery mildew while avoiding species-level overconfidence?
expected_points: White powdery patches that expand and coalesce across leaves, stems or buds are compatible with Cannabis powdery mildew.
Published hemp reports confirmed Golovinomyces-associated powdery mildew using pathogenicity testing together with morphology and sequence evidence, not appearance alone.

A photograph can support a powdery-mildew differential but should not assign a Golovinomyces species without appropriate laboratory identification because Cannabis-associated taxonomy has changed and closely related taxa can overlap morphologically and genetically.
forbidden_claims: White powder on a leaf proves Golovinomyces ambrosiae
A photograph alone can resolve the Cannabis powdery-mildew species

source_metadata.title: First Report of Powdery Mildew Caused by Golovinomyces ambrosiae on Cannabis sativa in Oregon

prompt: A legacy Grow Doc note says the Kentucky Cannabis powdery-mildew report proved Golovinomyces spadiceus is a distinct current species on hemp. Correct the claim and cite the source that explicitly discusses the later taxonomic interpretation.
expected_points: The 2019 Kentucky report originally identified the pathogen as Golovinomyces spadiceus using morphology and sequence data.
The later Oregon report states that earlier hemp reports labeled G. spadiceus are likely G. ambrosiae under the newer taxonomic revision.
Grow Doc should preserve the historical name for literature provenance while avoiding the claim that the older label is necessarily the preferred current taxonomic interpretation.
forbidden_claims: The 2019 name should be silently rewritten without preserving provenance
The older Kentucky paper by itself establishes the current taxonomy

prompt: Gray or brown rot is visible within a Cannabis inflorescence. Why should Grow Doc keep Botrytis as a differential but avoid calling every case Botrytis cinerea from appearance alone?
expected_points: Botrytis species are confirmed Cannabis gray-mold/bud-rot pathogens and can colonize inflorescence tissue.

Published Oregon work recovered more than one Botrytis species from hemp and completed pathogenicity evidence, showing that genus-level or symptom-level appearance does not uniquely identify B. cinerea.
Species confirmation should rely on plant-linked laboratory identification and pathogenicity-quality evidence where appropriate, while the visual observation remains a triage clue.
forbidden_claims: All gray mold on Cannabis is Botrytis cinerea
Bud-rot appearance alone identifies a Botrytis species

source_metadata.title: Three Botrytis Species Found Causing Gray Mold on Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa) in Oregon

prompt: A user uploads one photo showing stunting, chlorosis, white residue on some leaves and a browning flower and asks: 'Which pathogen is definitely causing all of this?' Give the safest evidence-based answer.
expected_points: A single image cannot establish that one pathogen explains all observed abnormalities.
HLVd, powdery mildew and Botrytis-associated disease each require different confirmation evidence, and mixed biotic plus abiotic problems are possible.
Grow Doc should separate observations by tissue/symptom, request cultivation context and fresh-sample testing, and avoid inventing a species-level diagnosis or causal chain.
forbidden_claims: One photograph proves a single pathogen is causing all symptoms
HLVd causes powdery colonies on leaves
Botrytis infection explains every stunting symptom
